utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric can you follow the proceedings in your mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones we are representing Mr. Naser Oric and we have Ms. Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant, and our CaseMap manager Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you and your team. Now, we have a problem. And we have to find a solution, basically. For reasons beyond our control, today we will need to stop before 1.00 to enable one of us to attend to a serious family problem. I know that this could in the end mean we would not be able to finish with this witness today. It should not be a problem because Judge Brydensholt and myself are prepared to continue with this witness tomorrow, just the two of us, and Judge Eser is -- agrees with this as well and this is what I would suggest that we do, if we don't finish today. I mean obviously. However, irrespective of whether we finish with this witness today or not, Judge Eser will be back or should be back for Monday's sitting and having discussed it a little bit with him and also with Judge Brydensholt, my preference, and it is basically also our preference, is that we don't start with the next witness in the absence of Judge Eser. I would rather have Judge Eser here from the beginning of the next witness rather than halfway through. So if we finish with Madam Hotic today, then tomorrow we are not going to sit. If we don't finish with Madam Hotic today we will sit, Judge Brydensholt and myself, tomorrow until we finish with Madam Hotic. We won't start with the next witness tomorrow and we will start with the next witness on Monday. This is the position. Any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this -- but believe me, there is no other way we can handle the matter, and we are trying to handle it in the best way possible. Yes, any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Bring in Ms. Hotic. Does it cause you an inconvenience? Because I see there was a little bit of discussion on --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what we are discussing is that another witness is coming and we calculated the time so that we would finish with these witnesses before the break on the 1st and 2nd so now we are talking about how to resolve this and we will do our best to find a solution. It's not a problem. But I think that the witness is already on his way and it can happen that the witness stays here for a couple of days longer than was planned, but this suits us and we will have a couple of days longer for preparations and that's how we will resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Madam Vidovic, and you will find the Trial Chamber very cooperative with you should you have -- should you encounter problems obviously. Same applies to you. I know this may disrupt your plans a little bit to a lesser extent. I agree. Yes, Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Hotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. You will not need to repeat the solemn declaration. It still applies once you have made it yesterday. We will be proceeding with the examination-in-chief and then later on you will be cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio. I forgot to tell you yesterday who we are, our names. I'm the Presiding Judge in this trial and my name is Carmel Agius and I come from Malta. Not the Malta which is near where you live but the island in the Mediterranean. Judge Brydensholt is -- comes from the Kingdom of Denmark. And Judge Professor Eser comes from Germany. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Jones [Continued]:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hotic. I hope you're well rested.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have some documents to show you this morning and we will start immediately with one which is a new document so we have copies to be distributed by the usher. Thank you. And this is for the record the ERN number is 04350699. That's the first -- the first ERN number of the first page and it's a document from the command of the first Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, report number 17 and it's dated either the 14th or the 17th of March 1993. Now, Ms. Hotic, I'll ask you to take your time to review this document and then I'm going to direct your attention to a couple of sections. First it's right, isn't it, that I showed you this document when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll direct your attention to first of all the first paragraph of this document and it's starting from basically the third sentence down. In English it says, "We occupied the Lalici-Sandici-Kravica line and established contact with our left-hand adjacent unit the Bratunac Brigade." We can -- just in passing we can see Lalici, Sandici, and Kravica on the map, D714. I'm not going to go to the map now. And then the fifth sentence, "The enemy has completely routed Srpska, Kravica which has always been ours is again in our hands. Successful operations of this kind by our brigade also give powerful impetus to adjacent units." And then I'm moving down to the next session, the heading of which is "unwelcome effects which mar the aforementioned achievements." And just for the record I'm going to read the first two sentences there, or three sentences. "Simultaneously with the successes and advances of our units there have also been unwanted occurrences and a stop must be put to them once and for all. Looting of anything found in the seized territory is rampant, cattle, television sets, video recorders, cassette players, different types of motor vehicles have been taken away. In short anything from a needle to a tractor is being taken away. These occurrences create a bad image of Serbian soldiers and onlookers get the impression that the Serbs are not fighting for freedom and survival but are rather looting hordes that take away and destroy everything in their path." Now, my question for you in relation to this document is the following: Firstly, when you were in Kravica on the 7th of January 1993, did you see Muslim civilians removing television sets, video recorders and other electrical items?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Kravica, people were taking food and perhaps if somebody found any clothing they took that as well because that was useful. There was a shortage of that, too. Other items, furniture and so on, that was completely unnecessary. It was worthless, nobody was taking that home. Even if they took something like that home, they had no electricity to plug in these appliances. But as far as people are concerned, if a person was hungry then it would be completely illogical [Realtime transcript read in error "logical"] for them to start taking anything else other than food. It didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One correction to the transcript. Did you say "completely logical" or "completely illogical"?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illogical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you lived through the winter of 1993 in Srebrenica. Can you tell us if there was much snow in that winter?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of snow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us roughly until when in 1993 there was snow, January, February, March, April, how late did it last?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was snow in April as well, and there was also a lot of frost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 7th of January 1993, did you see any houses in the Kravica area missing their roofs and thereby exposing the insides of the houses to the elements?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where, in which settlement? Houses in Kravica or in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kravica.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in Kravica, all the houses were intact, and I -- afterwards I didn't stay there for a long time. I don't know how long they stayed intact and whether they remained intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become Defence Exhibit D717. 718? 718. Thank you. Do we have by any chance -- I'm asking both parties, do we have a bird's eye view of -- photo of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think for our part we've ever produced such a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't recall having seen one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Neither do I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you, Mr. Jones. Can you describe Kravica to us? Is it a small village, a small town? A hamlet? How big is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kravica is a village of maybe about 30 to 40 houses. I'm not quite sure. If there are any hamlets that are part of the village, then they would be further up in the hills and I never went there so I really don't know what they looked like. The houses are scattered so there are gardens or fields between the houses. The houses are quite big. They are just normal houses that people live in. There are newer houses, older houses and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you aware of any particular communal buildings like the municipal building, the SUP or the town hall or the hospital or the school, if there is a hospital, I don't know, in this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that Kravica had anything like that. Perhaps it had the building where the local commune was but this belonged to the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Thank you, Madam Hotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the next document, Ms. Hotic I'd ask you to look at is a document of the 1st Bratunac light Infantry Brigade. With the assistance of one of the ushers, thank you. And it's dated 1st of April 1993, and the ERN number is 01319119. Since this is a short document I'm going to read what it says. It's an authorisation "issued to Zika Milovanovic, driver, approving the transport of goods to the vulnerable fighters of the Kravica battalion from Kravica to the Avdagina Njive of Daka's field sector and after the commission has completed the allocation of goods the distribution of these goods to fighters' families in Bratunac and its vicinity." Now, firstly, Ms. Hotic, have you heard of Avdagina Njive? Do you know of the locality?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Avdagina Njive but I'm not sure if this is from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bratunac towards Zuti Most. I might make a mistake there. I don't know the exact location of Avdagina Njive but I did hear of that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I simply want to ask you this: Seeing this document, and this authorisation from April 1993 approving the transport of goods from Kravica, does that strike you as odd or is that consistent with what you've told us and what you saw in Kravica, namely that houses remained intact presumably with goods inside them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Items, furniture, and appliances, that stayed because I'm sure that nobody took that. I'm talking about Muslims when they went on excursions to Kravica. Nobody took articles like that with them. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, unless there is something that's missing in the English translation, I don't see anything that identifies what these goods are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. The point -- MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I simply referred to goods. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, and that's all it says as far as I can see in the English translation. What these goods are could be rounds of cheers, tyres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They could be anything, I mean. MR. DI FAZIO: Hammocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the point is not in the nature of the goods. The point is, as my question alluded to, that houses remained intact and therefore the goods could be transported in April from Kravica. But I think -- I think that point has been sufficiently addressed and I'd simply ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be become Defence Exhibit D719.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document we have is from the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade Command dated 22nd of July 1993 and the ERN number of the first page is 04359425. Firstly, Ms. Hotic, do you recall me showing this document to you when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a lengthy document and since you've seen it already I won't ask you to read the whole of it again now. I direct your attention firstly just to what's page 2 in English a list of names. Actually it starts on the first page in the B/C/S. Are you familiar with any of the names of the people listed there? In fact, if I may be permitted to lead I don't think it's a crucial point. Stoja Savic, do you know Stoja Savic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Stoja Savic, also by the nickname Tandara. That's what we called her. She lived in the Rudarska building across the street from the SUP. She had a very pretty daughter. Her husband died before the war. I know Stoja Savic well. The other people here, I had heard of them but I'm not sure whether I know any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, during the war -- afterwards, did you see a broadcast with Stoja Savic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a television programme. I don't know exactly what time this was. This was when the food convoy set out for Srebrenica. Stoja came out wearing black on to the Bratunac road. She stood in front of the convoy and she laid down in front of the convoy, cursing and swearing, and using derogatory terms about Muslims, calling them balijas because they had killed her only son and she was not allowing the food convoy to enter Srebrenica. I note that Stoja never had a son. She only had one daughter and the daughter's name was Lepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to direct your attention to what's page 3 in the English and it's three paragraphs which actually starts at the bottom of page 2 in B/C/S. You'll see, Ms. Hotic, where it's written, [B/C/S spoken], that paragraph at the bottom. And I'll just for the record read those paragraphs. "Families are systematically moving into and returning to Fakovici. For this reason the Commission for Refugees works in the field in Fakovici every Thursday attempting to get as many families as possible to return to Fakovici. In Kravica preparations are under way to renovate houses by collecting material. In the first stage efforts being made to cover the buildings, to protect them from further damage, and when the repairs to the electricity network currently under way are completed, work will start to make these buildings habitable. It is expected that 20 families will return to their homes in Kravica by the winter." And then it's the next paragraph in particular which I'm going to ask you about. "When gathering construction materials several actions were observed that are not in the interests of the community. Roofs were removed from houses which could have been occupied, joinery and plumbing were ripped up and floors were destroyed. Because of this we would appeal to soldiers and the citizens of Kravica, Bjelovac, and Pobrdje to stop this practice, and in cooperation with the commission take this material from damaged houses that had been scheduled for demolition." Do you see, follow that passage, Ms. Hotic?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have a few questions. Firstly, perhaps an obvious point, but this is a document of the 1st Bratunac light Infantry Brigade. It's referring to citizens -- soldiers and citizens of Kravica, Bjelovac, and Pobrdje. Would this be referring to Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they address the Serbs. The -- because the Muslims were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied only to Serbs. Their own people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words this reference to roofs being removed, plumbing being ripped up, and floors destroyed by soldiers and citizens of Kravica, Bjelovac, and Pobrdje refers to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will become Defence Exhibit D720.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now after the action in Kravica, did the situation in Srebrenica improve or get worse or remain the same? The situation in terms of food and the refugee situation.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of food, yes, but it did not last very long, and in terms of refugees, the situation remained the same. There were too many people and too little accommodation and everything else was lacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness could be shown D581, please. And again, I'm just going to read a couple of sections. It's dated 10th of January 1993. It's a report of the War Presidency of Srebrenica. It says, "Aircraft again flew over and attacked the very centre of the town of Srebrenica. There were two sorties, one at 1515 hours and the other at 1520 hours. One of the aircraft dropped its deadly cargo. Two people were killed as a result and a few others were wounded. The material damage is huge." Now, pausing there, did you see in Srebrenica the damage caused to buildings by Serb aircraft?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with that description that the damage caused by such aircraft was huge?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going on to the second paragraph, "Yesterday and this morning the enemy was ferociously shelling the entire area of Srebrenica. Over 200 shells of the biggest calibre hit the industrial zone in Potocari alone. Three persons were slightly wounded, but the damage to the industrial facilities is enormous." Again I'm concerned with the amount of damage to property caused by these attacks. Would you agree that the damage caused by Serb shelling could be enormous?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was enormous. Not a single house in Potocari was spared. Houses were totally destroyed and the industrial area was totally destroyed, the roofs were taken off, basically, and you could see everything was ravaged, and I can only wonder how it was possible for anyone to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the third paragraph, "The aggressors opened fire at Osat [phoen] and Kragljivoda from their well-known strongholds in Serbia, the slopes of Mount Tara and the plateau of the Bajina Basta hydroelectric plant." Now, yesterday in the reference in the transcript was page 43 line 14, you referred to Tara as a stronghold. Is that the same reference? Is that the same place you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you also familiar with any firing or shooting from the area of Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the Drina, whether it was from Bajina Basta or closer, there were tanks there and other artillery weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, I would like the witness to be shown D571, please. This is a document of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality dated 11th of March 1993, and I'll give you a moment briefly to review that document. Now, in particular what I would like to direct you to is the second paragraph where it refers to thousands of women, children and the wounded arriving in Srebrenica from all sides. Do you recall that occurring in mid-March, refugees arriving, and if so, do you know where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the refugees very clearly. The refugees in those last villages, they too had to leave and come to Srebrenica, Osmace, Biljega, Osat, Klatuvac [phoen], all those villages. It was only in Suceska that was still held by Zulfo Tursan that they could stay because it was still in Muslim hands and all the other villages, as of the river of Drina and all the way to Srebrenica -- I mean they were so close, they were a stone's throw from Srebrenica, and they were already occupied and all the people were sent off to Srebrenica and quite a few people were killed and wounded and there were all sorts of things there. And Srebrenica was plagued by hunger any way and people had nowhere to go and so it was a disastrous situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that situation, do you recall whether people were suffering from fleas, lice, or scabies or similar ailments?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, due to a lack of hygiene, many people having to sleep and spend time together, at close quarters, of course, lice and scabies appeared, and all that is very catching, and we did have problems with that. There were fleas, too. There was nothing we could do about the fleas. They jumped every which way. And there were other diseases as well. It was horrific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in March 1993, if you saw an emaciated, flea-bitten, tired person seemingly unable to walk, was that anything out of the unusual? Sorry, anything out of the usual?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our daily bread and butter, unfortunately. We all looked like that. We were all emaciated and we were all weak, and were all the same. And I used to say that we didn't even know whether we were men or women. People lost all their characteristics, all their other features, except for this unending quest for food and the fight for survival. And at that time when we were subjected to horrific attacks from the enemy, we were in such fear that we didn't even feel like eating. I remember that some powdered milk was air lifted to us. And I was in Stari Grad and I basically stepped over a sack of milk powder but I could not even make myself take it because I expected to die any minute. And the news trickled through that one of our people heard on his Motorola that General Perisic from Serbia is ordering 13.000 soldiers to attack Srebrenica and make sure that not a single baby in its cradle remains alive. And it put such a fear into all of us that we could not even think of eating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that situation have an effect on the mental health of the population, the mental state, if you were able to notice?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that there were more or less or the same number of mentally unstable people in Srebrenica at that time, March 1993?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, my question was unclear. I meant --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few people who acted and abnormally, as it were. I never actually pondered whether it was due to the situation or simply due to the fact that many people were packed together but you could see people wandering the streets and they acted abnormally, total abnormally, almost like lunatics. Out of control, they were talking gibberish, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions for you, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Hotic but there will be questions from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Di Fazio, the break will be in an hour's time at 10.45. There will be half an hour's break and then we will sit again from 11.15 until 12.55. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you for that, if Your Honours please. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Hotic, my name is Di Fazio. I am from the Prosecution. I have some questions to ask you and, like Mr. Jones, I would appreciate it if you would keep your answers as brief as possible. A simple yes or a no will always suffice, and if I require further information, then I'll go ahead and ask you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one or two matters that arose from your evidence this morning. Just the very last point that -- one of the last points that was raised by Mr. Jones regarding the lice and fleas and scabies that were a problem and probably endemic in Srebrenica. Mr. Jones put a scenario to you as to whether or not it was a common sight to see people covered in those parasites who were, unable to walk. So not just covered in parasites but unable to walk. Did you see that very commonly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was also combined with the word emaciated. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and emaciated.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were the streets of Srebrenica covered with people lying in the roads, unable to walk and covered in scabies and lice?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's an unfair characterisation of her answer to make it appear as if it was a ridiculous answer. She was asked if she saw it commonly and she said "yes". That doesn't mean the streets were littered with people who were unable to walk and were covered in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's true. Perhaps now why she's -- she has heard the exchange between you and she can give us a clearer picture. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how often would you see it every day? How often?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often came across women affected by scabies but it doesn't mean that they were lying on the streets and totally unable to walk. They were starved, they were exhausted, plus they were plagued by these scabies so they had to scratch all the time. But it wasn't as if they were lying in the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that and thank you for that. Did you yourself suffer from any of these problems? Or any members of your family, for example, your husband or your sons?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only problem I could not really fight off was the fleas but since I was staying at my own flat and I did not really have to live in close quarters with too many other people I could defend myself from everything else. I did not have any scabies or lice but we did have fleas as well because there was just nothing we could do about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were suffering and your family members were suffering from this infestation of fleas or these problems with fleas, were you able to nonetheless try and carry on with your life and do the best you could in the circumstances, go out and gather food, speak to people, walk around, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes of course. I had to walk. I had to work. No matter how exhausted I was and how difficult it was but it was the only thing we could do in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned recently in your evidence, just moments ago, the use of a Motorola to inform you of Serb plans for some dastardly act, some bad act. What I'm interested in is not the Serb plans but who you heard this from and who had the Motorola.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly the name of the person that I heard it from but the news spread like wild fire through Srebrenica, about this general, some general called Perisic who was supposed to have issued such orders. But Motorola could have belonged to some former police officer, just the same as they had a couple of rifles. Those who used to be active police officers on duty before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you specifically connected the hearing this news with -- through a mechanism of a Motorola. Obviously it must have stuck in your mind because otherwise you wouldn't have mentioned it. You would simply have mentioned what you had heard. So what is significant about the Motorola? How did you come to recall that particular detail, the use of the Motorola to convey this information to you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had there not been for that Motorola nobody would have been able to capture that information because if you had no device, you could do nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know who owned the Motorola and you don't know precisely when this Motorola was used to gather this information that was later told to the population?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I could perhaps clarify this a little bit. Motorola might have been captured in some kind of action. But it did exist at the time. I don't know exactly who had it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One thing is absolutely clear. The Motorola was linked to the dissemination of this news in Srebrenica. It was the Motorola, that device, the radio device, that enabled the news to be heard and then conveyed to the people of Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether this was a piece of news that was being spread on purpose or whether it was just a leak like many others, I don't know, because you could just not keep any secrets at that time. Everything came out sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Okay. Now, I'd like to turn to your evidence that you gave yesterday and I'd just like to start off by asking you some questions about the shelling that you've described and you've described it at length throughout your evidence. You mentioned yesterday that there was artillery in Pribicevac a nearby hamlet or village to Srebrenica. In the course of your testimony you also mentioned mortars being located there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Pribicevac and you told us all about that episode with the man, Drago. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like to be absolutely clear about is this: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very clearly because that was my first contact with war, with fear, the first event of that nature. I remember Drago Andric from Pribicevac quite clearly. I spent a night in his house and I heard from him that a mortar was set up at Trkalija [phoen] and then they felt it was not the best solution and they were going to take it to Vakluvski [phoen] and they wanted to pound the Green Berets in Srebrenica from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for all of that. I heard your evidence yesterday as well and you clearly have a good memory of the matter. Now, what I want to know is this: The episode that you described with Drago involved just a mortar. Is that correct? Do I understand you correctly? The episode when --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a mortar at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Later you mentioned that there was artillery or it was suggested to you and I think you agreed with that, that there was artillery in Pribicevac. What I would like to know is this: Did you only ever see a mortar or mortars in Pribicevac or did you also see heavier guns, heavier artillery?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I didn't actually see but we were being fired at and they were using heavier artillery from that area that we could see from the marketplace at Srebrenica in the direction of Pribicevac. It was from there that they were firing and using other artillery weapons and there were some kind of PAM and PAT bullets, that's what they are called, and they came as far as the Srebrenica market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could see through a cut in the trees, some sort of path or cut in the trees in the hillsides. You could see that -- through that clearing, so to speak, up to Pribicevac; is that correct? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't need to see that clearly but you see a passage, a clear passage through the woods. The wood was cleared in an area which was a square area and from there you could hear the noise, the rumbling noise when they fired their weapons, and then of course you could see the explosions down in the town and then you could have a clear picture of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't let us be in any doubt, Ms. -- Madam -- Mrs. Hotic. I understand you perfectly. I understand what you're saying. What I'm concerned about is this: Could you actually see the guns that were firing? Could you see them with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the naked eye, it is impossible to see a gun in its entirety as such but when it is fired, you can see a kind of lightning and of course you hear the explosion, but from that distance, it is impossible to discern a gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could have seen a tank and sometimes you could see a reflection in the sun, and normally when they were in action, they would be brought forward and then when they finished their ammunition they would withdraw a little bit, and that could have been seen easily from other places as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, isn't it, that emplacement of guns in a place such as Pribicevac changed from time to time, the nature of the gun that might be there in that location changed, it might be a tank or a mortar or artillery, some days or weeks they might be there and other times they might not, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was something every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't actually know if the guns, judging on the flashes of light that you saw, were actually located in Pribicevac or some area away from Pribicevac, would that be correct? All you can say is that it came from the general direction of Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Pribicevac, well, there was some kind of weaponry on the same spot, whether it was guns or tanks, but it was always in the same wood clearing that could be seen from Srebrenica. Always the same spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was in the same spot? Actual guns, metal structures that --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Supposedly -- I suppose it must have been an important position for them that they had prepared, and they always used to fire from that position. It didn't have to be a mortar at all times. They had mortars in the beginning and presumably they proved to be inefficient or something, or they just got to reinforcements, but we were being pounded by these other weapons that I've mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Hotic, I'm not in the slightest trying to suggest to you that you weren't -- were not, were not being bombed, okay? I'm not trying to suggest that or get you to say that. My concern is only this: The location of weaponry in Pribicevac was something that you couldn't actually see, you don't actually know if the weaponry was located in Pribicevac or somewhere nearby or somewhere perhaps further afield from Pribicevac. All you can say is a that there was firing coming from that direction and that's based on your sighting of flashes. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well that question has already been put. Mr. Hotic [sic] is basically -- is insisting on this submission, that the witness couldn't see it. She's answered that she could see the clearing, she could see the flashes on the clearing, so to simply keep insisting that -- that she couldn't see what shes told us she saw is not a question. It's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She has -- I think the objection is a valid one. I would suggest to you, Mr. Di Fazio, that you either move to a different question or that, if you are -- you think that there is further clarification that is required from the witness, you put a different question from the one that you have put. Because to me she has actually made it clear where she had doubts, she said she had doubts; where she was clear enough, she said so. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there firing from the direction of Pribicevac or this clearing every day of 1992, from the time the war started, of course?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the direction of Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you could see the flashes -- yes. And you could see the flashes every time there was firing, every time --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was looking, if I was in a position to watch. Sometimes I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could just listen to the explosions. Because I was not in some kind of position where I could observe what was going on because I had to seek shelter as well, and it was not just from Pribicevac but from all the other areas that we were being fired upon. For example, from Bratunac, from Zvijezda, I was on my way to Potocari to get milk from people who had milk, and I saw clearly when a gun fired and the shell landed right in front of us and two girls were wounded. But that was on those occasions where I was in a position to see things, when I was heading in the direction of the place from where they were firing and at the right time because I wasn't always there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to another location of shelling. You say that you went to Sase and that was in the autumn following its liberation, autumn of 1992. Had you been there, to that -- to Sase, in that area, prior to your going there, that is from April to the late autumn?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that Sase was free, when the Serbs were no longer there, I went there and I said yesterday that that was when I saw a lot of shells, I saw a lot of cartridges of different sizes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We will get to those cartridges in just a moment, if you don't mind, but I would just like to remind you of your evidence. You were asked by Mr. Jones how you knew if the artillery was coming from Sase into Srebrenica and you said because shells were landing from that direction, and he asked you how do you know that. And you replied "on the basis of my sense of orientation. I know where that is and we could see the shells coming from that direction." Then you went on to say, "Obviously because Serbs were holding those positions that was quite clear, and it was clear that they were shelling us from Sase or from other surrounding villages or locations where they could place their weapons." So in the case of Sase you concluded that shelling was coming from Sase on the basis of the fact that it seemed to be coming from the direction of Sase and there were Serb positions there. That's it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because there were no Muslims in those places and there was nobody else who could shoot. It was the Serbs who were shooting at us and the direction from which they were shooting was Sase, Zalazje and some other nearby places. Later it turned out that this was actually so. That's the conclusion that everybody came to, all the people that I was with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, but the conclusion is based on the general direction from which the shells came and the fact that Serbs held those positions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you don't actually know if the shells were coming from Sase or Lasovac or Bjelovac or some position over in -- across the Drina in Serbia, do you, when you say that there was shelling from Sase. It was just that shelling came from that general direction, from Serb positions in that general direction, and that's what your conclusions are based upon. That's all I'm suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may respond, sometimes shooting was heard or sounds were heard when the shells were being fired, and that could not have come from across the Drina because it was too far away. You could hear them -- the sound as they were firing the shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that all you could say was that shelling was coming from the Bosnian side of the Drina, from Serb held positions, somewhere in the area of Sase? Would you agree with that? That's as far as you can really say. That's as far as you can really go.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that we were shelled from Sase and the reason is that -- I saw that for myself when I saw all of those piles of cartridges in Sase, that they had fired at us. So when I said that, I saw later that it was true, that they were firing at us from Sase and also from Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there are three factors that make you think that shelling was coming from Sase, the fact that it came, the shells came from that direction, the fact that they were Serb-held positions there, and the fact that months later you went there and saw shells. Those three things make you conclude that there was shelling from Sase, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt about that. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that all you can really say is that shelling occurred from the general direction of Sase, and that's really only -- the only conclusion you can draw, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would not be the only conclusion. I specified that later I could see for myself that there was no doubt that we were being shelled from Sase, from various artillery weapons, and I could see that on the basis of the shells that I saw, the cartridges that I saw there in Sase when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I understand. I'm not suggesting to you that -- I'm not suggesting to you, please don't get me wrong, I'm not suggesting to you that there was never any shelling from Sase. I'm not trying to get you to say that. All I'm asking you is this: When you were in Srebrenica and you're being bombed, and the shells are coming from that direction, you don't actually know if the shells were being fired in Sase or some other location four or five kilometres away or two kilometres away or three kilometres away from Sase. That's what I'm asking you. Did you understand? Now, if you insist that it was Sase, fine. But what I'm putting to you is that you can't actually say that.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were exposed to the shelling from that direction, I need not have known the exact place. But afterwards, when I went to those places and whether I saw where we were being shelled from, that's when I was convinced of that. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So as I take it, her conclusion was strengthened after she saw -- and I think we have -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's how I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want to make it even a little bit more clear. Let's imagine, Madam Hotic, that we draw a line as the crow flies from Srebrenica to Sase and beyond, and beyond it would be practically Biljaca in the same direction and Bjelovac is in the same direction. If you drew a line -- or Sikiric is in the same direction. If you drew a line, a straight line, from Srebrenica which passes through Sase and goes right to the Drina River, Sase is not visible with the naked eye from Srebrenica, is it? You can't see Sase from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. You cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any -- any mortars or any missiles that are arriving on Srebrenica from the direction of Sase could be fired from before Sase, from Sase, and from beyond Sase, and you wouldn't be able to know exactly whether -- where they are coming from except that they are coming from that direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then of course you eventually went to Sase and you saw all these cartridges, spent cartridges, and that reinforced your conclusion that you had been bombed from Sase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are clear. Let's pass to something different now. Unless you want to labour it any further. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I do there is just one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His Honour has taken you to the next topic you raised it yourself. The shells, the casings that you found or saw in Sase. Where in Sase did you see them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. It was out in the open at an elevation. I don't know how to explain that exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cartridges were not only in one place. There were several locations where there were piles of these casings, but that these piles were close to one another. They were perhaps a few metres apart, and the cartridges were of different sizes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Big ones, and small ones, big casings and small casings?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, for the record, if we could have an indication of what we estimate the largest of those gestures was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it necessary, Mr. Jones? Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It looked like a metre or so to me. MR. DI FAZIO: They were big ones, great big casings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At my home in Malta, I have got Second World War ones, I have a collection of them. They all vary in size. At the end of the day, I mean, that's -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, you don't actually know when those piles of casings accumulated this those locations, do you? You just saw them there?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we just move away from the -- from that topic, I want to ask you something about the shelling of Srebrenica. The shelling continued from May until at least April 1993. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave, and in the period of time leading up to the tragedy of 1995, was there more shelling?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think in May, perhaps I'm wrong about that but I know the weather was warm. In front of the school, people were relaxed, there was no shooting any more, the demilitarisation was in effect, there were no more soldiers, there were no more fighters. The weapons were taken away, confiscated. People were sitting around and they were playing some sports games. There were teams. I don't know whether they were playing football or handball at the playground in front of the school. Since the school was full of refugees with as many as 40 or 50 people sleeping in those rooms, even up to 100 people, but the atmosphere was relaxed and suddenly in the middle of the day, two shells hit that crowd of people. There were 70 or 80 dead. Those that were wounded and taken to the hospital later, 90 much them died and there were 200 people wounded. I ran out after the explosion. I was right there. And I thought, "My God is it possible that a person could have so much blood?" There were bits of flesh in the fence of the sports playground. There was pieces of brain matter all over the place. People were just loading up those bodies to take them away. And I know that there was information saying that there were 15 people killed, and I felt very sorry about that when I heard that, and I wondered, "Why did they state that number when they knew that many more people were killed?" I saw a little girl, her -- she was maybe four years old. Her body was completely ripped apart. Half of it was missing. I know that she was wearing a plastic sandal on one of her feet. I know that the explosion had shaken up a lot of people. The son of one of my neighbours was -- he had lost consciousness. This is what happened. There was another attack also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear because your question would cover both attacks. This one you have just described in detail to us, you said it occurred in May. Of which year? Because you didn't say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the first year of the demilitarisation. It was in 1993. I think it happened right away when the observers came, the Canadians were there. Please don't ask me about the dates. I know approximately the time and I know the events but I really don't remember the dates, even now I don't remember. I have to think about what happened yesterday or the day before. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Hotic thank you for your explanations. Look, I'll just make myself completely clear so that you understand. I'm not trying to get you to avoid the terrible carnage that you witnessed but my question is this: From demilitarisation until 1995, the events in 1995, was Srebrenica shelled continuously or frequently or were these just isolated attacks? No matter what the consequences were. Now, that's what I'm asking you about. How often? How often did it happen between demilitarisation and 1995?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't frequent in the town itself. It happened in the outskirts. There was some sporadic shelling. Sometimes there were mines, people were injured by mines. But this mostly happened at the elevations --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where the UNPROFOR had their locations. I can also say that about a month before the fall of Srebrenica, there was a fierce attack from the hill behind the hospital, during the night. It was an artillery attack, Zoljas were also used. That's when the apartment above me was damaged by a Zolja projectile and even though people from UNPROFOR were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there at the time, nobody retaliated. Two people were killed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you to contrast the period of time between May of 1992, leading up to demilitarisation in 1993. Now, that period of time, you say, don't you, that the situation was quite different in respect of shelling? Then the shelling was far more frequent, far heavier. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the start of the war until the demilitarisation, the shelling was intense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, not only was it intense, but it was all sorts of different types of shelling, wasn't it? That's what I think you've said. You --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. In the beginning, we were bombed by MiG airplanes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You're getting to one of the matters I wanted to ask you about, this air attack. You had MiGs bombing Srebrenica. You had Howitzers pounding Srebrenica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also multiple rocket launchers were constantly active. They could fire 36 shells in bursts of nine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And not only that but mortars as well?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'd agree that it was heavy, continuous bombing by all sorts of different type of military ordnance or shells?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just ask you one thing, if you allow me. In that period, I never put on pajamas in order to go to sleep, and I would never wake up in the same place where I fell asleep. During the night I would always have to go to a different place that was safer. I could not even be relaxed for a couple of hours at a stretch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In fact, in your evidence yesterday, in one of the answers to Mr. Jones's questions, you said, I think, that either when demilitarisation occurred or shortly thereafter, Swedes, and presumably part of some UN contingent, came in and repaired the buildings. You remember that? You remember that testimony? In fact, your precise words were, "they came in and fixed up the roofs and some of the holes, but it -- I" --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I gather it wasn't very much of a repair job but something at least happened, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite important. A house was unprotected without a roof. But when you patched up the roof then you would have shelter. So people did that. There were also a lot of timber houses in Jadar - I don't know exactly the place - so a large number of people could be Ahmo dated there. These are prefabricated houses. They were later used for Serb refugees after the fall of Srebrenica. You could even see those houses today. This really helped a lot in providing accommodation for the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, just remind me, just tell me, is Jadar a suburb or area close into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You pass through Srebrenica in order to reach Jadar. It's about ten or 15 kilometres away, perhaps more. I didn't ask, or I never actually knew exactly how much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly turn to another topic now. You would I think agree with me, wouldn't you, that in Srebrenica in 1992 and early 1993 and probably thereafter just about every single commodity that you can think ever was -- there was -- there were shortages and in addition, some commodities were simply not available at all. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree, wouldn't you, that the infrastructure that existed in Srebrenica was struggling to deal with the problems faced by the population. For example, the hospital had troubles finding medicines, if they could find medicines at all? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We didn't have any at all. As for electricity and water, even after the demilitarisation, we were still without electricity and water. It's true that the people from UNPROFOR made it possible to have water for bathing. It was a special healing water and it made it possible for us to heal the scabies that we were suffering from. So that was good for that. But it wasn't water that was good for washing clothes or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the normal civilian organs that you'd expect in a peace time society, they were all having troubles functioning, if they functioned at all. For example, the police?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that police was formed at all during the war and also during the demilitarisation period. I don't really remember that the police existed at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it that there was no effective and functioning fire brigade in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I take it there was no functioning or effective fire brigade functioning in Srebrenica, a fire brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, there was, but then it was only the UNPROFOR that had the means to deal with that. They were everything to us at the time. They were the authorities, the police, they performed all of these functions. We were just ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that the UNPROFOR people came in, at the time of demilitarisation in early 1993, Srebrenica hadn't burnt down, had it? It was damaged but it was damaged by bombs.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica was burned. You can see the traces of that even today. Never mind when the UNPROFOR came. Even to this day, you can see soot on buildings from that time. Srebrenica hasn't changed much from that time. There hasn't been much of repair work since then. There are still traces of burning and bullet holes. People, it's true, have started to renovate their houses a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I have absolutely no doubt that in 1993, if you had walked through the streets of Srebrenica, you would have seen a scene of devastation. What you would have seen though is bomb damage, not burnt out buildings, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. Most of the buildings in Srebrenica were damaged by torching. The bullet holes are not so difficult to fix, but once a building has been torched, that's even more difficult. The roofs are missing, walls and everything. And another thing, all the Muslim houses, all the buildings, were burned 100 per cent, even the chicken coops. Not one single house remained intact. The Serbs set them all on fire. Wherever they came they would burn everything and they left nothing behind them. This is something that I am stating with full responsibility and many others can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact you'd seen torching, hadn't you, using your binoculars from your position, or the binoculars of your friend?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you'd seen Serbs, hadn't you, torching houses prior to their abandoning or leaving Srebrenica, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Srebrenica burning. After the demilitarisation, I could go to the villages and I did go there because we went there to look for fruit and other things. We returned to the Muslim villages to see what the situation was, to pick fruit and so on. Not a single house was standing there, or any other building, of course the same goes for Srebrenica and I could see Srebrenica when it was burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last ten minutes or so I've been asking you about Srebrenica. That's what I'm interested in. I know what you said about Serbs setting fire to houses in May. I've heard your evidence and I know that you saw it and you described how they set fire to the houses and the houses burnt down. Now, apart from those houses, apart from those houses that were deliberately subject to arson attack by Serbs, apart from them, I'm not talking about them. Apart from them, in 1993, when the UN forces arrived in Srebrenica, the overwhelming damage that the township of Srebrenica had suffered was the result of bombing, not fire. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't agree. A lot of damage was caused during the bombing, but most of the damage was caused by fire, because even if a shell does hit a house, it doesn't knock it down completely. Glass would shatter, there was no glass any more or windows, but this is something that can be repaired. But once a building burns down, then it's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can add one more thing. Apartment houses were not burned, probably because there was a mixed population, both Serbs and Muslims, living there. I'm talking about apartment houses where you have more apartments. But all the Muslim single-family houses or something like that, they were all burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just not quite clear about your last answer. Are you suggesting that the Serb shelling deliberately avoided apartment houses because of the possibility of Serb families living there? I don't want to put words in your mouth but is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She will explain it, Mr. Jones. If she doesn't then obviously I will intervene. But for the time being, let her, let her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about setting buildings on fire. I'm not talking about shelling. When you're shelling, you can not pick and choose. When a plane is bombing, they just unload their ammunition or shells. They hit wherever they fall. Even the church was damaged, the Serbs probably didn't do that intentionally but when you want to set something on fire then you know exactly what you want to burn. Apartment houses were predominantly populated by Serbs. In my apartment house, there were eight Muslim-inhabited apartments and 16 apartments inhabited by Serbs. I don't know why but mostly the apartment houses had more Serb tenants than Muslim tenants. These buildings were maybe damaged by shelling but they were not set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- I need clarification now at this point because in answering your previous question -- Mr. Di Fazio, let me go to the previous page. Yes. A couple of minutes ago, Madam Hotic, you said, "I can add one more thing. Apartment houses were not burned. Probably because there was a mixed population, both Serbs and Muslims, living there. I'm talking about apartment houses, where you have more apartments. But all --" this is what I'm going to ask you about. "But all the Muslim single-family houses or something like that, they were all burnt. They were all burnt." So my question to you is this: At the moment of demilitarisation, 1993, how many or roughly what percentage of Muslim single-family houses were still intact? Because you're saying all. I take it that you don't mean exactly all from number 1 to number whatever. But were there any left intact or not? At the time of the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you. The houses in the border line areas, the end of the Crni Guber street, the last houses there, were not torched because they were very close to the forest. And, well, maybe a couple of other houses remained intact. I can't give you the exact percentage. But several houses, several houses, remained intact. And as to apartment buildings, Serbs were not living in those buildings at that time because the Serbs left when the Serb population left Srebrenica. So they were not inhabited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just from that last question from His Honour, you said, in talking about the percentage of houses in the -- in Srebrenica, that the last houses in the borderline areas were not torched. Now, all this damage to Muslim houses that you've been describing, is that the damage that you saw taking place by Serb men on the ground in Srebrenica prior to the withdrawal of Serb forces from that -- from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not quite clear to me. I mean, the damage I witnessed, I told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. You told us about what you saw from through the binoculars up on the hill. I've heard that. I've understood that. I think everyone has. There is no problem with that. You're quite clear about that. Now, were all the Muslim houses that you know of being destroyed in Srebrenica, were they destroyed then, back in May, when you were looking through your binoculars down on the town, is that when the Muslim houses were deliberately torched, set fire to, and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of May 1992. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, May --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that first torching, no houses were set on fire in Srebrenica any more. They were damaged by shelling but they were no longer being set on fire because they were under our control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honour just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just while we are talking on this burning of houses, in the early part of 1993, you've told us already about the Muslim houses, do you know if they spared Serb houses, not apartment blocks but Serb houses? Did they spare them when they were laying -- setting fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge -- very well, the point is being raised. It's not in early part of 1993. MR. DI FAZIO: Slip of the tongue and I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'll just repeat it because I misled you perhaps. I'm talking about 1992, the same occasion when you were looking down through your binoculars down on to the town, okay? Now, on that occasion when houses were torched by these Serbs, the Muslim houses, did they also burn Serb houses or did they presumably deliberately spare them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some Serb houses that I knew of remained intact. They were not burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house next to the church, and something else in the centre of town, I know they -- those houses which were left standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I want to turn now from this issue of shelling and damage to another topic, please. And that is the question of clothing. You said yesterday that, in answer to a question from Mr. Jones, that it was -- you couldn't really distinguish between men in fighting units and civilians, and you gave the example of your own son who I think had trainers and he didn't have military uniform. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that my son used to wear a pair of jeans and a jacket and some sneakers. Most of them were dressed in that way. Perhaps some were slightly better dressed and others had torn clothes. It depended on what their possibilities were. People who came over, they had the clothes that they had on their backs when they had to run. So mostly civilians, I mean civilian clothes. There were no uniforms whatsoever, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's clear from your evidence that you went to Fakovici, Bjelovac and Kravica. On those occasions, did you see any men -- by that I mean Bosniaks, men on your side -- walking around with ribbons? Ribbons either tied around their forehead or their arm or somehow attached to them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Maybe I wasn't paying enough attention but I just can't remember. I'm unable to tell you either yes or no. It just--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what about Kravica? Apart -- I'm not asking about ribbons now. Did you ever see any men in -- fighting men, wearing white uniforms, white coverall, overall uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Next to the hill of Jaglici. Since the snow was white, you could spot people walking like they were ants, you know. Against this white background they looked like black ants, all of them, whether you wore brown or grey clothes or blue or whatever, but there was this white snow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour there is one correction for the transcript. The witness said "to tell you the truth," she didn't just say "yes," as it seems to look in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Still we haven't got an answer to the question. The question was: Did you see in Kravica, did you see men wearing, I will use exactly the same words used by Mr. Di Fazio, white uniforms? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honour pleases, fighting men, I qualified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fighting men wearing white uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. MR. DI FAZIO: I think this is the time, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a 30-minute break and we will resume at 11.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. You may proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We were talking about uniforms. Now, you earlier today and indeed yesterday you said that commodities were generally in short supply. One of the most precious items that could be had, apart from perhaps food and medicines or perhaps equally with food and medicines, was a weapon. That was correct, wasn't it -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, the fighting units needed all the weapons they could get to hold the Serb forces at bay, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified that -- when you were talking about Torbari and Hapsi, and in the context of Fakovici, that some of the people who went into the villages, the civilians, had rifles. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any pressure by those in charge of the fighting units to try and commandeer, get ahold of these weapons from civilians it would had them?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighters were volunteers. Whoever wanted to fight joined in and for the most part people wanted to join in and join in the defence. Whoever had a rifle was more desirable as a fighter. And in every action, even, you know, people who were fighters occasionally were not fighters all the time. At times they were fighting, at other times they were just looking for food. It depended on needs and on their goodwill. Nobody made them do anything or coerced them into joining the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one that you saw in Fakovici or Bjelovac or Kravica, who was armed with a gun, was a civilian, were they? They were all members of fighting units. Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said not always, not in the course much every action. Sometimes they were fighters and on other occasions they were not. If they didn't want to be and if there was no need for everyone to become an active fighter on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me approach it this way: Would you agree with the proposition that anyone who was carrying a gun at any of these actions that you've talked about must have been a fighter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make it clear that you're restricting it -- whether you're restricting it to Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not have to be the fighters. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear whether you're still referring exclusively and only to Fakovici, Bjelovac, or Kravica, or whether you are extending it to any other actions. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think we need to be clear on this. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- I'll repeat my question. And to be more precise, as His Honour has suggested. Would you agree with the proposition that anyone who was carrying a gun at Fakovici, Bjelovac or Kravica must have been a member of a fighting unit, given the scarcity and the shortage of weapons? Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not really clear to me. We seem to be talking about one and the same thing for the third time, and I don't see --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
