utterances.text: All right. Well, you gave lots of evidence yesterday. Mr. Jones asked you many details about the people you call Torbari, okay, the civilians who went into these places and you also have talked about fighting men, men, for example, like your son who was a member of Hakija Meholjic's unit. My proposition is a very simple one. What I'm saying is this: Because of the guns, because of the scarcity of guns and the fact that you're surrounded by hostile Serb forces, any man who had a gun must have been a member of some fighting unit. Now, whether it was Hakija Meholjic's unit or Zulfo Tursunovic's unit or someone associated with Mr. Oric or whatever but they must have been a member of a fighting unit. Do you agree with that conclusion? Is my thinking correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would just like to explain this. I can't answer this by yes or no, because if a person has a gun, that person may act as a fighter in a given action but does not necessarily need to participate in any action as a fighter, even though they may be carrying a gun. Sometimes they may be going along just in order to look for food and they may carrying their weapon -- they may be carrying their weapons just for self defence and they did not have to relinquish those weapons even though there was a shortage of weapons because there was no law or regulation in force on the basis of which people could be forced to relinquish their weapons or to become fighters just by virtue of the fact that they were armed. It was all voluntary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not suggesting that the fighting men in the fighting units were not volunteers. Did you actually see, with your own eyes, at Kravica or Bjelovac or Fakovici, people you call torbari gathering food and carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see people carrying weapons and carrying food as well. I didn't actually ask them whether they were participated in any fighting or whether they just went along to get the food. There was no need for me to know and to be honest, I wasn't even interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can understand that and you would have to agree with the proposition, wouldn't you, that those people that you saw might have had a dual role on that particular day, they might have been fighters having finished their fighting and they might have been set about gathering food, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both things could happen. They might have gone along only and exclusively to get food or else they may have participated in fighting and then went on to look for food afterwards. I didn't need to know but, yeah, presumably that could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Let's move to the topic of Fakovici itself. Yesterday you said that you arrived at Fakovici at about noon, about midday?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before noon.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The attack on Fakovici started about noon or in the middle of the day. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack started earlier because there was shooting down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So is it the case that you can -- you simply don't actually know when the fighting actually started? All you can say is that at around noon or midday when you arrived, fighting was already underway?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there, fighting was underway, because I could not see any people with guns around me. They were already in action. So fighting was underway, there was shooting, and I waited for a while for the fighting to abate, in order to enter the town. But then I said I could not go in due to the firing of bullets from the opposite direction and, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you left Srebrenica to walk to Fakovici along with all the other civilians, the people you called torbari, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other people used to call us like that but we didn't mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite a walk, isn't it, from Srebrenica to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several hours, but I never actually timed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, I don't want to be pedantic but can you give us an approximation, two or three or four hours? Have you got any idea?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three hours roughly speaking because it's through the forests and hills and it's not really a welcoming terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with or do you have any reason to dispute that the attack or the action, let's say - I'll use the word action - action at Fakovici occurred on the 5th of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you have the exact dates I'll probably agree with you but I can remember the dates myself. Or, if you have it from some other source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. And you'd heard about this attack, you say, by word of mouth and that you -- news of --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: News of the attack essentially spread through the town, you say, by virtue of the fact? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- fighters told presumably their families. Is that what you're saying? Is that how you came to know of the attack?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never knew for sure how we came to know about it. There was no public announcement or anything. It was an open secret, as it were. It was supposed to be confidential but everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what precisely did you hear on the grapevine? Did you hear that the attack was fixed for two or three days' time? Did you prepare for it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we would get to hear about it on the eve of that day. We would normally be told there is going to be an action somewhere tomorrow and then of course we would get ready to leave as well. We just went without any consideration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You had -- you had to plan for it, didn't you? You had to get yourself ready, get your few meagre possessions that you had for the trip, get yourself dressed as best you could and calculate when you'd start walking and when you'd arrive at the place, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the preparations were not really so much. You would maybe put on some heavier clothes, get a bag and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But -- I appreciate that, but you had to make some sort of planning for it, didn't you? You had to know, for example, when to arrive at the scene of the action. That was important, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early morning, mostly. That was -- that was usually the time to go, in the early morning. By the time you get there it would be day already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Hotic, but that's not precisely my question. What I'm interested in is not when you went but this: You had to know -- you had to know fairly clearly when to leave in order to time your arrival at the scene of the action. You would agree with that, wouldn't you? Wasn't that essential in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly we knew that we had to leave as early as possible. Some people would get there earlier. Some people would get there later. I think at the time I was a bit late in getting into the village because people before me actually went in before the shooting because of which I was prevented from going in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Fakovici is a perfect example of this, isn't it because if the attack had been timed, for example, to be a nighttime attack or late dusk attack, you wouldn't have had to set off at dawn, would you? You could have set off perhaps later in the day. That would have made more sense, wouldn't it? But in fact Fakovici the attack did occur around the middle of the day and so you timed accordingly. You left early in the morning, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The objection is there are so many questions there I'm not sure which one the witness is supposed to answer. She may agree she left earlier in the morning it would then seem to be she was agreeing she timed her departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, please choose which question you want the witness to answer first because it may dispose of the others. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fakovici -- in order for you to leave at dawn or early in the morning, really early in the morning, to get to the scene of the action, you must have known approximately what time the action was going to occur.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the actions were carried out early in the morning for the most part. I didn't have to be there during the action. That was dangerous. So I was always afraid and I would always get there later because many people were wounded, many people were killed, those who would go in right away. It was very dangerous to do that while the combat operations were still going on. Perhaps I wouldn't find as much as the others and I would leave with less but I would never go in amongst the first. I was always a bit cautious in such cases. The action had to be completed. There should be no longer any danger of shooting. There should be no fighting. And then after that I would go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely I mean because again I don't think the witness has answered your question. In order -- you have given a very clear explanation now but, to me, this means that before you could decide or you would decide when to leave Srebrenica to go to Fakovici, necessarily therefore you knew what time roughly the attack would take place. Because you, as you explain it, you were intent always in trying to avoid being there during the action itself. So you had to know what time the action was going to take place before you decided to leave Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less. Not the exact hour, the exact time of attack. It often was the case that I would wait a little bit farther away until the danger was over so that I could go in. So that means that I could arrive before the action was completed but not go in. It happened like that this time. I was picking plums, eating plums, eating grapes, close to where I was supposed to be but I was not exposed to so much danger. I cannot say that I always knew exact -- the exact time but it was in the morning. Whether this was at 5.00 in the morning, 4.00, 3.00, sometime after midnight, that's something that I didn't need to know. I never knew the exact time. It was just morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A further question and then I leave -- give you back to Mr. Di Fazio. In these instances, the attack on Fakovici, on Bjelovac, on any of the attacks where you went to collect food, would you know when the fighters would leave? In other words, was it also common knowledge amongst the people in Srebrenica, the fighters have left now at 3.00 in the morning or the fighters have left now at 5.00 in the morning? Or wouldn't you be aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that. I never had the opportunity to see the fighters leaving. I never saw that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may not have seen the fighters leaving in preparation to leaving to go off to their attack, but did you know what time they were going to leave so that you and other civilians could time your arrival?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what time the fighters would leave. I didn't see that, and I couldn't always know something like that. Even when my son was leaving the house, sometimes he would go to his friends' and he wouldn't even say anything to me. He wouldn't say goodbye. This happened also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really appreciate if you would give me a brief answer so we can move on. Just give me an approximate number of the people you call torbari who gathered at Fakovici. Are we talking hundreds, thousands? What sort of numbers?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking thousands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, for thousands of people to arrive at Fakovici early in the morning on the 5th of October 1992, would have caused a catastrophe, wouldn't it? Because they would have arrived there before the fighters even got there. If the attack started around midday, you would agree with that, the only possible consequence was a catastrophe, unarmed civilians gathering at the site of an attack before it's even occurred. Now would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a large area. People would spread out. They wouldn't take just one path through the -- people would go through the fields, through the forest. They would be spread over a wide area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So they would approach not as a group? That's what you're saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were groups. They would arrive in groups. But it would not be a group of 1.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be 200 or 300 people in a group, and they would approach from all possible sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would have to agree, wouldn't you, that even if they are approaching, indeed because of the fact that they are approaching in groups, civilians from all sides around Fakovici - this is the scenario I'm asking you about, if they arrived in such a manner before the fighters even got there - or even started their attack, the Serbs would have known instantly what was going to happen. Now, you'd have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were coming in such numbers would not go into the town. There were forests, different places to conceal oneself, to stay low. So that you wouldn't be noticed. It was a large area and the configuration of the terrain was such. Everyone was aware that they had to be quiet so that they wouldn't be noticed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of how many of us there were. There were always more of us than the people who were participating in the action, who were going to take part in the combat. There were always many more of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you receive instructions, I mean you and/or the other people you call torbari. Did you receive instructions on how to make your approach to the scene of an action? For example, to do what you just said, lie in hiding?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive instructions from anyone. Each person was aware of that. They simply felt that they had to behave like that only a fool wouldn't behave like that. Everybody was taking care of themselves. They were taking precautions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. We have been looking at the scenarios for the torbari preceding the attack. Let's look at the situation after an attack. I think you've said -- testified that people would go into the areas that had been subjected to an attack or an action, whatever the correct word is, and keep on gathering food and so on. Do you remember that? Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was therefore important for the people you call torbari to try and get into the place as quickly as possible following an action in order to get as much food as they could secure and get out of the place as fast as they could. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I agree that people, when they went in, I'm not speaking specifically about Fakovici because I wasn't there, but in other places where I was, people or large numbers of people would be grabbing things from each other, taking things from each other's hands, in order to be able to put that in their own bag. So sometimes people would be grabbing the food and the food was collected quickly so that people could leave as quickly as possible. It was also possible that these places could be shelled, and the Serbs would often shell these places while people were still inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's even more compelling reason, isn't it, to coordinate your actions with those of the fighters, isn't it, to avoid precisely the scenario you just described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object to this question. There have been a line of them, where basically the witness is being asked for want of a better word, to speculate. It might not be the best word to use in this context. But in essence, Mr. Di Fazio isn't asking, Did you coordinate, did you and others do X, Y and Z, it's wouldn't it this have been a good idea wouldn't this have been necessary, wouldn't that have been necessary, and my objection is on that basis that this witness can say whether they did actually coordinate their actions and coordinate their watches, et cetera, and I'm sure we will know what the answer to that would be whether it's important whether it would be a good idea that's an entirely different matter and I don't think that's even really admissible testimony from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. Partially, however, because at the same time it could then elicit a more reasoned explanation on the part of the witness. In other words, depending on what she is answering until now, if it's put to her that perhaps a more rational approach to the whole exercise would have been to have someone -- I don't like -- wouldn't like to say much, then she can I think explain if that was the case, or, if it wasn't the case, why it wasn't the case, or why it couldn't be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes it's a question really of keeping the two distinct, what they actually did and what would have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, there I agree with you that's why I said I partially agree with you. But the question itself is not irrelevant or misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just should perhaps alert that I would then probably Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have a fairly lengthy re-examination to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are at your disposal, Mr. Jones, I mean, and Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just as to exactly what did occur, right, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Let me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you consider -- did you consider, you personally consider, timing your arrival at the scenes of these actions to avoid getting there too late and possibly avoid retaliatory counterattacks, Serb attacks? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the question is clear to me, it would always be uncertain when I went. No one could coordinate these things. We are talking about large numbers of people, and as I said, there was no open talk about it. But it was still known. We went because we needed to get food, and because of that, we might have interfered with the fighters during the action because it was also necessary to pull out the wounded, to take out the bodies, and so on. That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely why you're being asked these questions, because in reality, you are now telling us that there were -- there was more to it than just going there following or not following the fighters in order to be able to be there once the fighting was over to collect, gather, as much food as possible. There was much more to it. There was involved, as you rightly point out now, the question of not interfering with the fighting, with the fighting plans and with the fighting itself. Not to obstruct it. I mean, so at this point in time, given that there were these other considerations that were in play, irrespective of whether it's being organised or coordinated or not, but where you put on notice, for example, the population as such, was the population put on notice that if you are going to proceed to do -- to the place where the action was going to take place or has taken place, you should avoid interfering with the operation itself? Or with the action itself? Or was everyone left to do what he or she liked? I mean, as you explain it, I take it that you decided to go to Fakovici not in agreement with others but at your own decision, and you would leave your home at a given time, you decide yourself. And it's only by chance that along the way you meet with these several hundreds or thousands of other people going in the same direction. That's how you have explained it to us so far. But was more to it than that? This is what you're being asked to answer. And I think I've tried to explain myself in a simple manner. Perhaps you can try to answer us in a simple manner too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very complicated question. It's so convoluted. What I said was that there could not have been any coordination between the fighters and the torbari people. If we torbari didn't go, we would be left without food. If we were to listen to them and not disrupt them, we would not get any food because they couldn't bring back any food. Fighters, if they brought back any food they would bring back food for their families. They couldn't bring back food for everybody and what would the rest of us do. And they couldn't prevent us from going because how would they explain to us why we should not try to get any food? Simply it was a kind of implicit agreement. Everybody did what they had to do. I mean, I can't give you another answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that what in fact happened is there was a degree of coordination between the fighting units and the torbari, that there must have been some sort of communication between those two groups, the people you call torbari and the fighting units, in order for you to be able to, within reason, within reason, safely carry out your food-gathering exercise. Do you agree with that proposition or not?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say this: It was never safe for us, and I was always aware of the risk, and I took the risk. I couldn't ascribe that to anyone else. There was no coordination. There could have been no coordination. First of all, all of our fighters, our defence, was not united. Everybody waged fights on their own terrain. Sometimes it was a joint action. Sometimes it was on their own terrain. Sometimes it wasn't possible amongst themselves to be coordinated, never mind in other cases. This all happened spontaneously. It evolved from moment to moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. When you actually got into the -- into the houses and places that you went to in Fakovici and Bjelovac and Kravica, you went into houses looking for food and so did the other people you call torbari, right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you came across boxes of ammunition or grenades or helmets or submachine guns or Zoljas, were you expected to do anything with that sort of material? I'm not suggesting this actually happened to you but what I'm asking you about was, had you received any instructions on what to do if you came across such valuable material?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any instructions in case I came up with something like that. I would always look for food in places where I assume that food would be kept. So I don't have any such experiences. I didn't have anything to do with weapons and I don't know what I would have done if something like that happened. I never really thought about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that wherever the Serbs were, there were -- words to this effect, I don't think I'm misquoting you, that there were weapons' dumps, collections of ammunition and so on. Weaponry. Before you went out to these places, did it ever occur to you that you, you, Mrs. Hotic, in the course of your going through houses, might come across something as valuable as a gun, machine-gun, or landmines, anything, something like that? Did you ever give any thought to that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never gave it any thought. Obviously, all villages where there were Serbs had weapons. They had weapons in their homes and in warehouses. That was a generally known fact. It was common knowledge. But presumably in the course of the action as the fighters went in before us, they would have taken care of it. So I never had the opportunity to come across any weapons when I went looking for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "presumably in the course of the action the fighters went in." Do you take you to mean that presumably the fighters went in and scoured the houses for such material, weaponry?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously it was something precious. We had no weapons and that was the only way for us to get arms and to be able to defend ourselves. It was a must. There was no choice. Basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact ever run into such dumps or caches or, if not collections, even isolated weapons?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just came across empty crates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And sometimes there were scattered in front of houses. It was elsewhere, in other places. And I did mention that I went looking for food 19 times, either after the military action or without any action, just sneaking through the Serb territory, through the fields, trying to pick some produce, up until the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Hotic, I saw you holding your back. If you have any problems, I won't be able to tell but if you do, please tell Their Honours and alert them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mrs. Hotic, do you want a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm a bit cold because the air conditioning is blowing cold air onto my back. But that's the only problem. But it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't want any witness to feel uncomfortable. So could we either lower the air conditioning a little bit? I don't think we can switch off the ventilators. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, do you feel able to continue?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no trouble. Don't worry, everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can stop and you can have a coffee, if you want to warm up, and in the meantime we try to adjust the climate control here. Or the temperature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No worries. Everything is fine. It's not a major issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you happen to have any other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you happen to have any other clothing in here, which you can -- would like to put on, we'll give you the opportunity to do that. Do you have a coat or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's fine. It's fine. I don't have an overcoat or anything but, yeah, it was just a gesture I didn't even think about. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, if you need assistance or if you need a break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- please let us know. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So am I correct that if you had come across such material, you wouldn't have known what to do? You wouldn't have had any instructions or general directions on contacting, say, for example, the commander of your son's unit or a local fighter who might be standing around in the area and inform him or her -- him that you found this military material?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are just assumptions and conjectures, because even a commander or some other leader would not have time to say anything. I mean, had we come across anything like that, some men would probably get their hands on that stuff earlier on and I wouldn't even have the opportunity to touch it or go near it but it has never happened anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were alerted to the possibility of -- you were alerted to the possibility of weapons -- not weapons so much, more ammunition, being located in the Serb houses because according to you, one fighter, a fighter, told you that it was dangerous to torch houses because of that fact, because ammunition might be inside the houses. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wasn't given that warning myself individually. Fighters might have talked about it amongst themselves and they must have reached a conclusion that it was hazardous, which indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you were a little more emphatic about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have the reference from yesterday and it was, "sometimes I would hear the fighters say it was very dangerous to torch a Serb house. " That's her evidence, not that she was specifically told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I recall as well, actually. Thank you, Mr. Jones. That's how I recall it. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was mentioned on more than one occasion to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wasn't mentioned to her. I mean, that's not how I read it. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is overhearing fighters say so. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you overheard from fighters on a number of occasions about that danger?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard it, overheard it from the fighters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fighters ever give you any other tips on what to do, how to handle going through houses, other than that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, it's a mischaracterisation, again, a two-fold mischaracterisation. Did give any other tips? Well, that wasn't a tip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other advice, advice?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But she has never said that the fighter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- gave her any advice in the first place. It was by chance or not I wouldn't know. But it so happened that she overheard fighters saying something. Now, perhaps what you should ask is whether you -- whether she overheard fighters or anyone else saying something else related to what you would like to know but it doesn't seem to say that at any stage she has said she was given advice what to do and what not to do. MR. DI FAZIO: I appreciate that. I'll rephrase my question. I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever overhear any other fighters making observations in respect of torching of houses? I think that's fairly neutral.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I had never heard any talk about the torching of houses except for the point I've already mentioned that it might be dangerous if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was ammunition in those houses and that whilst we were in the area it was dangerous to do that because it was simply impossible to tell people to get out and get away because the people would stay there until they've searched everything and then I don't know what happens next. Every one, when they got the stuff they needed, as much as they could carry, we would go back as soon as possible. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time you were in Fakovici, Bjelovac or Kravica, did you ever see any man apparently from a fighting unit or any member of the group you call torbari deliberately setting fire to any structure, barn or house or any other structure in those places?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with a great deal of certainty that I have never, ever seen anyone torching anything. I did mention that a haystack was on fire at Kravica, but who set it on fire and how I don't know. That's all I can say about torching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hakija Meholjic expressed his views to you, to you personally, regarding torching, didn't he, or burning of houses, and he said, "Don't burn houses, we are going to need the houses. Where are the people going to be put? The people will come, they will have a house," page 73 of the transcript. "They will have a house, they will have a field, they can work the land". This is something I "actually heard from him personally."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, again there is a distinction between something which she overheard. This is something that I actually heard from him personally. I heard about Hakija Meholjic, who had issued orders to his fighters not to burn houses. I'm looking at that. And Mr. Di Fazio a moment ago very specifically said, he said -- expressed his views to you personally, didn't he? Again that's not a fair characterisation of what she said. Again it's a question of overhearing rather than her being specifically told something. It's an important distinction. Important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we can simplify this. I suppose you have the extract from yesterday's -- MR. DI FAZIO: And there is not a single word in that about overhearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You read it out to the witness verbatim, please, as it is in the transcript, even though it's not yet official and then you put the question and we'll see what the position is. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll also put Mr. Jones's question just so it's put into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Question from Mr. Jones: "Did you -- let me put it this way: Did you ever hear a conversation, conversation, in which fighters spoke out against burning, burning houses or a specific fighter?" Answer, "I heard about Hakija Meholjic that he would issue orders to his fighters not to burn houses. He said, 'Don't burn the houses, we will need the houses. Where are we going to put all of these people? They will come. They will have a house. They will have a field. They could live there and work the land.' This is something that I actually heard from him personally." I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question now. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when and where did you hear Mr. Meholjic saying these things?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion in Stari Grad, he was talking to a group of his fellow fighters and he gave that advice to them but he wasn't addressing me, in fact. So that's with reference to what you've just read out. He did not address myself. He was simply giving advice to his fighters against the torching of houses in that way and he also explained that we would need those houses in order to house the refugees and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I understand how you heard it. Now, having overheard this from him personally, can you give us a time, an approximate time, you overheard it in Stari Grad. Can you tell us if it was in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us the context in which you heard it? Was it at a meeting or a casual comment that you heard --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was an aside. It was not during a meeting. They were just having an informal conversation. I happened to be there and I overheard it. I was in Stari Grad quite often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason -- withdraw that. I suggest to you that at the time that Mr. Hakija Meholjic made the aside that you overheard personally, there had been a widespread practice of the burning of Serb houses during the course of actions such as Kravica, Bjelovac, and Fakovici, burning by the people you call torbari and by the men in the fighting units.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really and truly know nothing about that. I have never heard anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It must have stuck in your mind because if it was just an aside, it's not likely that you would have recalled such a matter many, many years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The -- it must have stuck in your mind, it presumably is that Hakija Meholjic made a comment, there's a danger that that's suggesting that widespread burning must have stuck in her mind or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it as I understand it, at least the way I heard Mr. Di Fazio myself. It's Mr. Meholjic's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps the question is why she recalls it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. It could have been put in a simple way. Why do you -- why has it stuck in your mind? Why do you still remember it after so many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably because I valued his opinion. I thought that this suggestion of his and this warning of sorts was quite correct. And that's why it stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the time you heard Mr. Meholjic say these things, had you heard at least rumours about houses being burnt, Serb houses being burnt, during attack by Muslim forces or units or fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I never heard anything about it but maybe it was just not mentioned but I really and truly never heard any mention of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. She's back to you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something? What I did here, what was crucial was to neutralise the positions from which we were being fired at and get our hands on some food and to get as many Muslim villages back as possible in order for people to be able to go back to their homes because Srebrenica was just too small for all of us. Yes. I could hear those comments. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. You've got more than half an hour left. In fact, you have got 35 minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry if you don't finish today. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm just informing for the Court and for Mr. Jones, I'm just looking at my notes, I think I may finish in the time so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- yesterday you said -- Mr. Jones had asked you questions about the very fact of your going to these sites of actions and you said that the fighters in Srebrenica were opposed -- were opposed to civilians going to such locations.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, just again to avoid any misunderstandings, I'll read out the testimony word for word. Mr. Jones asked you there question: "And again, as far as you knew or were aware, were the fighters in Srebrenica came that you and other civilians should go to Kravica or were they opposed or were they indifferent? What was the position?" And you said, "They were opposed. The fighters were opposed. First of all, they were even opposed at the idea of launching an action against Kravica but the people insisted, they kept begging them to do something."

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might be a typing error. Then it goes on: "You said you have to do something, you must do something, otherwise we'll all starve to death. What is this fate that has befallen us? Nobody actually believed in a good outcome but it was a must. We were forced to do it." You recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to understand that portion of evidence clearly and I'm certainly not seeking to put words in your mouth but are you saying that the idea of an action at Kravica was discussed by the people with the fighters? Is -- am I correct in your understanding -- in my understanding or not?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because there couldn't have been any other contact, any different contact. You wouldn't have been able to find out in any other way. People were putting fighters under pressure. They were saying, allow us to get to Kravica, make sure that we can get some food and for days they would be put under pressure in order to launch this action to enter Kravica in order to make it possible for us to get some food even though we were all afraid that it would be very difficult that there were would no doubt be victims. But it was a matter of life and death and death was basically certain, death from starvation. It was horrific. It was indescribable. And I don't think anyone would have decided to launch this action against Kravica had it not been so horrible because we were all afraid of that. We were certain that it was a real stronghold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So I'm correct, then, am I, that the situation was so bad it was in the middle of winter, people were starving, it was cold, and all the other terrible conditions that applied, and so the people, by that I gather you mean people in Srebrenica and in the safe -- Bosniaks living in the area, encouraged, urged, the fighting units to attack Kravica to secure food and ward off this starvation that was impending?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the discussions last or how long was the topic alive, at least in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly for how long it went on but this period, this very difficult period, went on from the end of the year, the end of December 1992 and the beginning of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the month of January. I don't know the exact period but it was very long. And then we exhausted all the supplies, babies were dying of hunger. We couldn't even come up with a single spoonful of flour there was no sugar, no salt, no fats of any kind, no spices. As I said, you couldn't even get a single spoonful of flour and this whole mass of people was living there. I don't remember exactly for how long it went on but the situation was certainly horrific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we have a little bit of a confusion with the dates leer because reading the transcript it says, "this period, this very difficult period went on from the end of the year, the ends of December 1992, and the beginning of 1991." So I think we need -- when did this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps I misspoke. Sorry. I meant 1993. If that's my mistake, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on this particular occasion it couldn't have been a question of you finding out about the attack on Kravica just shortly before. It was a topic that was being discussed in the community. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was there any discussion on this occasion as to how you torbari would behave on the day of the attack on Kravica? Was there any discussion with the fighting units, any that you're aware of, at least?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about anyone talking about how we should behave. Perhaps somebody else knew. Perhaps such conversations took place elsewhere but I myself did not talk to anyone about that. I found out Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about the attack on that very day when the attack was launched because in the early evening I went to Kravica and basically the attack took place in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were the commanders of the various fighting units consulted or spoken to about a potential attack on Kravica? If you know. If you don't know, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never talked to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps she can tell us actually who took part in these discussions between the members of the people of Srebrenica and the fighters? Were there representatives -- because I would imagine there were representatives from both sides. Are you aware of this? Would you confirm it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean meetings being held or something? No. Perhaps it was in smaller groups. I mean everybody knew a fighter or two. Everybody had someone. I really don't know in what way it was done but I do know that people were clamouring for that. I mean, we just heard about it like we heard about everything else. I don't know specifically of any meetings or any talks having been held. I really don't have any knowledge about that. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I think I'll be able to wrap it up fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last topic I want to speak to you about, ask you questions about. That's the actual -- perhaps two topics I want to spoke to you about. You said when you went back to Bjelovac, on the second day I think it was, that you went back to Bjelovac, that you were at a place called Loznicka and that you went into a house and there you were subjected to some sort of bombing. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you either misspoke or that it was translated wrongly. When the action in Bjelovac happened I happened to be in Loznicka Rijeka at the time, not in Bjelovac. I went to Bjelovac the day after the action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you had that written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shelling in the area of Fakovici as well. I talked about that yesterday. And a shell struck a house where I was getting food. I think you probably have that written down as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, again would I ask Your Honours just to given me a moment's indulgence just while I look at the transcript. All right. So on the first day, could you actually see Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could just hear the fighting going on over there, quite intense fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you didn't know your way around that area because you hadn't been there before the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went with the other people, but I didn't know any of the places myself. Before the war I would take the road through Skelani. That was all. But before the war I didn't really know many of the villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you -- on the second day when you went there, did you actually go into the town of Bjelovac or the hamlet or the village, call it what you will, of Bjelovac, or did you simply go to an area of houses close to what you thought was Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the area of Bjelovac. I was just in their fields. I assumed that there was no more food in the houses because I had gone the day after. So I went to the fields in the area of Bjelovac. At the time there was firing at Kunjerac, it was the hill of Kunjerac close by, and as I was collecting food, picking corn in a corn field, there was an airplane in action at the same time. I think I mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I show this witness this map and I'd like to seek to tender it. It may be of help in the future as well. Perhaps if it can just be put on the ELMO. I think this map is probably big enough, Madam Hotic, for you to pretty quickly see the area that you're talking about. You see Bjelovac there and Kunjerac?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Loznicka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, looking at that map --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that map and seeing where Bjelovac is located and you can see the road going straight through Bjelovac, okay?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, through Bjelovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking at that map --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could I ask you, perhaps if I hand you a pen, to mark with a cross the area that you think that you were in on the second day, the second day, not the first day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near these crossroads. That's where the fields were. This intersection leads towards Sase through Zaluzje and Voljavica. This way it's Bjelovac, Sikirici, and the other places. So I was there at this intersection in these fields near the Drina River. That's where I was picking corn. The houses were mostly along the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please draw a circle around the area where you were saying you were on the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around here somewhere. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think the pen works. Thank you, if Your Honours please, I seek to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spent the night here, somewhere in one of the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you put your initials against or inside that circle, please? MR. DI FAZIO: I got a better pen here if the usher needs it. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we give it a number? An exhibit number? I've lost count. This will be P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be P565, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. P565. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to remind you of your evidence, yesterday you said in answer to questions to Mr. Jones that you were in the area of Bjelovac and he asked you if you saw houses in Bjelovac on that day and you said you saw some white houses but you didn't go into any of them, and you didn't notice any signs of burning. I take it that you meant you didn't see any signs of burning on the white houses that you saw in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The houses that I saw were white. I mean, I didn't notice anything else. Had they been burning, they would have looked different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kravica now. I will be brief. You got to Kravica towards the end of the day, I think, and it was dusk, right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the spring, yes. Sorry, it was dusk yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's -- it was January the 7th, 1993. Just assume it was early January 1993, okay? You may not know the precise date but assume it was early January 1993 it would have been pretty dark, pretty early, wouldn't it, probably got dark, what, around 4.30, 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, but there was snow and the visibility was good. It wasn't dark because everything was covered with snow. So I think that provided some additional illumination. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you got there in -- I think your words were dusk. I think that's the word that you used yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twilight -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twilight or dusk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- was the word used. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's correct, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- after walking quite some time in order to get to that location. And in fact you had to make use of the burning haystack in order to see, to help you on your way?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to have the light from the haystack because when I went to the house to get food, I could clearly see the house itself as well as some outbuildings that were around. I could see clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, I think you must be wrong about that. Because yesterday you said -- Mr. Jones asked you, "Did you see any objects which had been on fire," and you said "Hay was on fire but it provided light for us so we could see where we were going. That was the only thing that was burning." So the haystack did provide light for you, didn't it? That's what you said yesterday so I assume that's still so.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not the entire road. That part was lit well. I walked fast. I didn't stay in that place. I didn't ask myself why the hay was burning. I was just on my way to look for food. I passed by a couple of houses. I got to a stream and then I came to a house. It seemed new. It was looking very nice. But I didn't go into the house. Some women went into that house. So it occurred to me just to go to these other buildings, and I found some food there and I collected as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then got out of the place as fast as you could, right?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I went up the hill, using the same road that had been walked by all the other people. It was busy, people were going to Kravica, returning from Kravica. Everybody was content though they were all carrying food. There was food. We were very happy about that. It was a pleasant surprise for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it must have become very quickly night by the time -- on -- by the time -- when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't have had any good view of the houses in Fakovici, would you? Because of the fact it was night time. Sorry, Kravica. My apologies, Kravica.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went home, I didn't look back at Kravica. I just wanted to leave and go up the hill, and I wanted to avoid the shells that were coming from the hill. MR. DI FAZIO: Madam Hotic, thank you for answering my questions. If Your Honours please, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there any re-examination Mr. Jones? Re-examined by Mr. Jones:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, a few questions. I think I should be able to fit in depends on whether Your Honours have any questions but I certainly can finish by 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't enquired with I think Judge Brydensholt or Judge Eser -- do you have any questions? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I can probably be about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can basically take the entire ten minutes left here, if we can send her home without having ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That would be ideal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you I will not stop you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hotic I just have a few questions for you and if you could answer them as concisely as possible then it will be easier to finish in the allotted time. Firstly, you were asked today about houses which were burnt in Srebrenica in May 1992. Just so we are clear about what you mean by Srebrenica, one might consider that Srebrenica starts at the boundary with Potocari and goes right up to Crni Guber or we might consider Srebrenica is just the town itself. When you were talking about burnt houses in Srebrenica, what part of Srebrenica were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was talking about the urban part of Srebrenica, and that's from the gas station up to the top of the Crni Guber street and to the top of Petrici and Stari Grad. That is the town of Srebrenica. When I'm talking about the Srebrenica villages, then I mean the surrounding settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now today, and it's just -- for everyone's reference it's page 47 line 18, when speaking about Fakovici, so I'm asking about Fakovici now, you said, quote, or you referred to "firing of bullets from the opposite direction." I just wonder if you can help us with what you meant when you referred to the firing of bullets from the opposite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. direction in Fakovici. From which direction?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant from which side I was going to enter Fakovici. It was in -- the bullets were coming more from the left side to this part of the road that we needed to cross. So that I and the group of people that I was with did not manage to cross that part of the road because it was exposed to fire. Perhaps it wasn't exposed to fire when some other people were passing there. I don't know where the shooting was coming from. There were bursts of fire, not shells. But you could hear the whizzing sounds of the bullets as they were striking the surface of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were also asked today about the whole issue of whether civilians going into actions were coordinating their departure time to arrive when the action started. So I just have a few questions on that subject. Firstly, did you - you personally - did you time your arrival at an action at a precise hour, for example you knew that the action would be at 9.30 a.m., and so you arranged to arrive there at 10.00 a.m., or you knew it would be at 11.00 a.m., and therefore you planned to be there at 12.00? Was it anything like that precise?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never able to know how long I would need to get somewhere. All I knew was that we had to leave early in the morning. I would usually go with my friend Ismeta. I think I talked about that yesterday and there were other people too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not the case that you and thousands of others of you synchronised your watches and planned to all arrive at the same time?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did many people have watches in Srebrenica in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people did have watches. My husband had two, a pocket watch and a wrist watch. My son had one. Most of the people had watches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave that. Now in Kravica you arrived after the action. In Bjelovac you arrived when the action was still going on, Fakovici when the action was still going on. Isn't it -- is it correct that in fact civilians arrived at all different times during an action? They arrived before the action, during the action, and after the action? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. When I left to go to Kravica, I was already meeting people in Potocari coming back with a full load and they were telling us that there were many things there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people arrived before the action, is it right or is it not correct that they could actually wait until the action began?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Nobody dared to enter a Serb area before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did people ever actually arrive, even the night before an action? Is that something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you referred to going always in the morning, is it that you were informed on different occasions that an action would be in the morning or you based yourself on the assumption that actions would take place in the morning?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actions were usually carried out in the morning. This was common knowledge. So it was like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred or you were referred to the fact of the danger that civilians in actions would interfere with the fighters. Would you agree that you were -- that you collectively, torbari, were a nuisance to fighters if you were present during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of that but we had to get food. We couldn't expect the fighters to bring us food, and even if they did bring food they would bring it for themselves. They were not loading the food on trucks. They were carrying it on their backs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that, civilians were present during the fighting in all these actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the fighting, afterwards, they would go in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that in fact --

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the only way to survive. I think that this was characteristics only -- characteristic only for this region during the war. I don't think that it was like that in other places. Perhaps it was but cut off from the main command, without command, without any experts, without a proper army, condemned to death in advance. I think that scientists should study how we fought in order to stay alive. I think that probably this is something that will be examined. I'm sorry for speaking a little bit more about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. It was also put to you that there would need to be coordination between the torbari and fighters in order for civilians to be safe during these actions. Was it actually safe for civilians in any of these actions?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never safe. Each one of us was aware of that but we would pray to God and walk along the road and hope for the best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions. For Kravica, you were asked today about how people were put -- speaking to fighters about attacking Kravica. Is this something which was discussed in a formal setting to your knowledge, were there actually sort of meetings or a congress or was this something that people on the streets -- just discussing among themselves what needs to be done?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the houses where people were staying, on the street, there was no particular place such as an institution or something where people were gathering together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In houses, in the street, wherever we were staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In relation to that I want to explore this use of the word torbari. It may be a bit like one of those nouns like "the proletariat" which refers to a lumpen mass rather than an actual entity. Let me put it this way: Did you have a spokesman? Was there a spokesman or a representative or a committee or a council of the torbari who would speak with fighters?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was nothing like that. We perhaps called each other that. It was black humour. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it describe anyone with a bag in an action?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You couldn't live without bags. I sewed countless bags from cotton cloth or from parachute fabric. I made so many such bags in the shape of a rucksack or other kinds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions. You said that there was opposition to attacking Kravica because it was considered so deadly and frightening. Why, then, was a move to attack Kravica if it was such a deadly place, Kravica as opposed to some other location?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Everybody considered it to be a strong Serb or Chetnik stronghold. Kravica was thought to be a dangerous place, even before the war, in peacetime. People did not like to meet people from Kravica. People from Kravica would often provoke quarrels in cafes and so on. Kravica had a reputation for being a Serb or Chetnik stronghold. Bratunac was close by and they were connected with Serbs, with Serbia, they were well-armed. So it was important to us to get food. That was the only reason why we went to Kravica. It was because of hunger, because of food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will continue until we finish. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned how the action took place on Orthodox Christmas. Did that have any bearing on the amount of food which was expected to be captured? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I don't see how these issues arise out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not hugely controversial but I just don't see how it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't need to insist on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I think it's -- you are right, definitely, Mr. Di Fazio. But on the other hand, it's a more or less harmless question. MR. DI FAZIO: I know but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can move on to another question which is a related point on Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was put to you that you actually knew of the action beforehand in Kravica because you, the torbari, or civilians, were putting pressure for there to be an action in Kravica. When did you personally actually learn that there was going to be an action in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out on the morning of the attack, sometime in the morning. And then I thought first of all, if I could go at all, because it was dangerous. Nevertheless I decided to go and I went there with my friend Ismeta, who was much braver than I, and I didn't make the wrong mistake -- I didn't make the wrong decision, because I did collect a lot of food. But I found out about it that morning, because it was known that the action was going to take place but not which day. Perhaps other people found out about that before me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just two final questions. And this is at page 74, lines 3 to 4 of the transcript, and this is referring to Bjelovac. In English, the translation was that you could here of hear the fighting going on over there, quite intense fighting. I believe that in Bosnian you might have said something more like the fighting was terrible. Could you just in a word or two describe the intensity of the fighting in Bjelovac as you could hear it when you were in Loznicka Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such terrible intensity of the fighting made me think that it would be impossible for people to stay alive there. The earth was shaking. When I managed to reach safer ground in the area of Brezovica, we planned to sit down, Ismeta took out some cheese and peppers and she told me to eat and I told her I couldn't. I was still shaking from the fighting. It was really terrible. The artillery, the airplanes shooting from firearms. I just thought that everything would be destroyed to the ground, and that nobody would manage to survive over there. Some civilians were killed there. I already talked about that horse here. It was really terrible. It was the heaviest fighting that I had ever heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, and sorry if I'm skipping around, but going back to Kravica it was suggested to you essentially that because it was winter and it was dusk, that you weren't able to see objects in Kravica. Were you actually able to see houses, roads, hills, and physical features when you were in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I recall the path, I recall the small creek, and the houses. They were very clear. I said there was snow on the ground. It wasn't such a dark night that you couldn't see anything. It was twilight. It wasn't completely dark. I could see the houses were intact. I passed from one house to the next. I even remember a place where meat was being cured. I could even see people taking the smoked meat from that smoke-house. I could see that it was a new house, there was a summer kitchen there. I think that even the summer house had a roof on one side, that there were two doors. In front I found a plastic rope to tie my crate to. And I remember that this rope was blue. It was easy to see it in the snow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, I take it it's not controversial that of course you can see flames, even when it's dark. You mentioned seeing flames from haystack. Did you see any other flames that day?

utterances.speaker: KADA HOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see flames except at the entrance when I saw that hay. I didn't see anything else burning. Nothing else was burning then, really. People were all over the place and nothing was burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have -- we don't have any questions for you, Madam Hotic, which means that we have finished with your testimony here. And that you will not need to come again tomorrow. On behalf of Judge Eser, who for personal reasons had to leave, Judge Brydensholt, and myself, but also on behalf of the Tribunal in general I would like to thank you for having come over to give testimony as a Defence witness in this case. Very soon you will leave this courtroom and I can assure you that you will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of everyone present here, may I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and thank you for making it possible for me to come and to tell this part of the truth. What I have told you here really is the truth. But if I were to tell you all of my experiences, it would be a lot to talk about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can accompany the witness. So the position is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was going to mention something about witnesses. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's first let the witness leave the courtroom. Bye-bye, Madam. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's just this: That since we are not sitting tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we need to sit we will sit at well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not -- it's really just to state the approach which we are taking with our witnesses which is that we have one arriving tomorrow who would be testifying next week. If we don't sit on tomorrow, then if we have Monday and Tuesday for the first witness that's scheduled, it's possible that the witness after that will be examined in chief and maybe partly cross-examined on Wednesday but then of course she would be in The Hague, I believe Thursday and Friday and into the next week. We personally don't have a problem with that but we just wanted you to know that that's how we will be approaching it so that -- that lest it be suggested that we shouldn't have started with a witness on Wednesday when it's clear that she might have to go over to the following week. That is the approach we are adopting because we wouldn't want to lose Wednesday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The idea was to have the next witness testify tomorrow and Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Current plan, if we were sitting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then the next one would sit on Tuesday and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tuesday and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, precisely so, and if we lose a day there is a possibility she'll go over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So witness number 2 will be testifying now Monday and Tuesday, I would imagine. Witness number 5 will be testifying Wednesday and Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but we are not sitting on Thursday, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why aren't we sitting on -- Thursday is the 1st of September. Yeah, we are not sitting on the 1st of September, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For what it's worth, our estimation of that witness is that she's not going to be unduly distressed by or inconvenienced by remaining here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we could do is this. Let's do it this way: That I haven't seen the summary of that particular witness so I'm not really in a position to gauge whether I would prefer Judge Eser to be present all the time so -- but we could tentatively work on this agenda. I definitely would like Judge Eser to be here for the entire testimony of the next witness. There shouldn't be a problem with the testimony of number 5 if we decide and agree that on the 1st of September we sit, the two of us. In other words, if I see that there is no potential prejudice, then we could start with Judge Eser with us on Wednesday and then continue to sit on Thursday without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This is the problem. For the time being, you will need to bear a little bit with us because we have a problem in hand and there are very few options available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly we are happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that we do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's perfectly fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that I will convince Judge Eser to go ahead, for us to go ahead without him. However, I have this caveat: I want to see what that particular witness is going to testify about so that -- because to be honest with you I'm prepared for the next one but I'm not prepared for the other ones. I need to check that. All right? And I will come back to you on Monday when Judge Eser will be back with us in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and of course, I should say we sympathise with the difficulties of Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are trying to ride the -- this as best as we could but it could get, we could have problems. Let's put it like that. We could have problems. So-- which were not anticipated unfortunately. So we will adjourn until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
